title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description: Brute force to optimized: downhill search from every individual cell versus two reversed multi-source searches from the ocean borders.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an m by n heights grid representing an island (the Pacific Ocean touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges), water flows from a cell to an adjacent cell with height less than or equal to its own. Return the list of cells from which water can reach BOTH oceans.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","heights grid"],["Output","Cells that can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic"],["Key Insight","Reverse the problem: search UPHILL from each ocean's border cells; a cell can reach an ocean exactly when that ocean's reversed search reaches it"],["Constraints","Up to 200 by 200 grid"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Can water starting at a cell reach a border, flowing only downhill (or equal)?\"","Reversing the search direction (searching UPHILL from the border, instead of downhill from every interior cell) turns this into a manageable multi-source BFS/DFS problem"]]}

blocks.text: Instead of checking, for EVERY cell, whether water flowing downhill from it eventually reaches each ocean (an expensive check repeated per cell), REVERSE the direction: start a multi-source search from ALL of the Pacific's border cells simultaneously, spreading to any neighbor with height GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO the current cell (since water flowing the OPPOSITE, forward direction from that neighbor down to the current cell would be valid). This directly identifies every cell that CAN reach the Pacific. Repeat separately for the Atlantic's border. Cells reached by BOTH searches are the answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracing Which Mountain Slopes Could Drain Into a Lake, by Working Backward From the Lake
blocks.text: Picture determining which points on a mountain range could have rainwater drain down into a specific lake, by working BACKWARD from the lake's edge, uphill, to every point that could possibly feed into it, rather than simulating water flowing down from every single point on the mountain individually.

blocks.caption: Reverse the flow direction: search uphill from each ocean's border; a cell reaches an ocean if the reversed search reaches it

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Checking, from EVERY individual cell, whether downhill water flow reaches each ocean border would require a separate search per cell, an expensive repeated computation.

Observation 2: REVERSING the direction, a multi-source BFS/DFS starting simultaneously from ALL of one ocean's border cells, spreading to neighbors with height GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO the current cell, directly identifies every cell water could have flowed FROM to reach that ocean, in a single combined search.

Observation 3: Running this reversed search once for the Pacific's border and once for the Atlantic's border produces two boolean grids, marking which cells can reach each ocean respectively.

Observation 4: A cell reaching BOTH oceans is exactly a cell marked true in BOTH grids, found by a simple final combined scan.
This leads to two multi-source BFS/DFS searches (one per ocean, traveling uphill from the border), then intersecting the two result sets.
For every individual cell, search downhill (to equal-or-lower neighbors) to check if a path to the Pacific border AND a path to the Atlantic border both exist.
Why the code is written this way

items: Searching downhill from every cell directly checks the definition of "water can flow from here to the ocean".
This repeats a full search from EVERY cell, costing O((rows times cols) squared) in the worst case; reversing the direction lets ONE combined search per ocean cover all cells at once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((rows times cols) squared) worst case, a search per cell.
Space: O(rows times cols) per search.
Limitation: reversing the search direction lets ONE combined multi-source search per ocean (not per cell) determine reachability for every cell simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Create two boolean grids, pacific and atlantic, both initially all false. Seed a multi-source BFS (or DFS) starting from ALL of the Pacific's border cells (the entire top row and entire left column) simultaneously, spreading to any UNVISITED neighbor with height GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO the current cell (the reverse of the downhill flow condition), marking each reached cell true in the pacific grid. Repeat separately, starting from ALL of the Atlantic's border cells (bottom row and right column), marking reached cells true in the atlantic grid. Finally, scan the entire grid and collect every cell marked true in BOTH grids.
Use two multi-source BFS/DFS searches, one per ocean, traveling uphill from the border; the answer is the intersection of both reached sets.

codes.python:
from collections import deque

def pacific_atlantic(heights):
    rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])
    def bfs(starts):
        visited = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        queue = deque(starts)
        for r, c in starts:
            visited[r][c] = True
        while queue:
            r, c = queue.popleft()
            for dr, dc in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]:
                nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
                if (0<=nr<rows and 0<=nc<cols and not visited[nr][nc]
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]):          # UPHILL (reversed) spread
                    visited[nr][nc] = True
                    queue.append((nr, nc))
        return visited
    pacific_starts = [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)] + [(0, c) for c in range(cols)]
    atlantic_starts = [(r, cols-1) for r in range(rows)] + [(rows-1, c) for c in range(cols)]
    pacific = bfs(pacific_starts)
    atlantic = bfs(atlantic_starts)
    return [[r, c] for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols) if pacific[r][c] and atlantic[r][c]]

blocks.text: Water flows from a HIGHER (or equal) cell to a LOWER (or equal) neighboring cell; reversing this, searching from the ocean's border UPHILL to neighbors with GREATER OR EQUAL height, correctly and exactly identifies every cell water COULD have originated from and flowed down to reach that specific ocean, since the reversed search retraces every valid forward flow path in the opposite direction; running this once per ocean (not once per cell) and intersecting the two resulting reachable sets directly finds every cell able to reach BOTH oceans, with no redundant per-cell searches.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols), each cell processed a constant number of times across both searches.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the two visited grids.

blocks.text: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow is a hallmark example of the "reverse the search direction" technique: searching from a small set of border cells outward is far cheaper than searching from every interior cell inward.

items: Searching downhill from every individual cell instead of reversing the direction, leading to unnecessary repeated work.
Getting the reversed condition backward (should be height GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO the current cell when spreading uphill, not less than or equal to).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single cell grid","That cell trivially touches both oceans (it is on every border simultaneously)."],["A completely flat grid (all heights equal)","Every cell can flow everywhere, so every cell reaches both oceans."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "reverse the search: start from the ocean borders and search uphill, instead of searching downhill from every cell" is the single most important insight for this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can flow (only downhill) from a cell reach multiple fixed destinations", think: reverse the search, starting from each destination and searching uphill instead.

items: How would you extend this to three or more "oceans" (destinations), still using the same reversed multi-source search technique?
Rotting Oranges and 01 Matrix, other multi-source BFS problems, though without this problem's unique "reverse the direction" twist.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The per-cell downhill search costs O((rows times cols) squared) worst case; the two reversed multi-source searches cost O(rows times cols) total, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: reversed multi-source BFS/DFS, searching uphill from each destination's border.
Core Idea: a cell can reach an ocean exactly when that ocean's reversed uphill search reaches it; intersect both oceans' reachable sets.
Time: O((rows times cols)^2) worst case for the brute force, O(rows times cols) for the reversed-search approach.
Space: O(rows times cols) per search for the brute force, O(rows times cols) total for the reversed-search approach.
Most Important Observation: reversing the search direction turns per-cell searches into just two combined searches total.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately tricky medium-level graph problem.
One line memory trick: search uphill from each ocean's border, intersect the results.
